sections.text:
The LORD opens with a tender sentence: “I have loved you”. And the people answer with a shrug. “How have you loved us?” That is how this whole book goes. God speaks, the people talk back, and God replies, round after round.

It is a quarrel among people who still belong to each other. God says the priests despise his name and bring second-best offerings to his altar. Marriages are broken faithlessly. Tithes are held back. And some have decided that serving God changes nothing: “It is vain to serve God” The proud seem to do well, they say.

But the book does not end in argument. It ends with a promise. A messenger will prepare the way before the LORD. And before the great day of the LORD, the prophet Elijah will come: “He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers”.

The book belongs to the fifth century before Christ. The temple had been rebuilt, and the early hopes that came with it had faded, which may be why the people sound so weary. The name Malachi means my messenger and may be a title, not a personal name, so we know little about the writer. It is the last of the twelve shorter prophets, the final voice before the New Testament begins in most Christian Bibles.

The New Testament applies the promised messenger to John the Baptist, and Christians generally follow that reading. They differ on one other point. Some hold that the book's teaching on tithes sets a rule for the church. Others think it reflects how the temple and its priests were supported, and they point out that the New Testament asks instead for generous and willing giving. Neither side doubts that the book calls God's people to honest worship and faithfulness.
